title: Probability, statistics & uncertainty
summary: Reason about uncertain events, conditional evidence, distributions, and estimates from samples.
html:
Reason about uncertain events, conditional evidence, distributions, and estimates from samples.

Probabilities describe a model of uncertainty

A probability is between zero and one, and mutually exclusive exhaustive outcomes sum to one. A random variable assigns values to outcomes. Discrete variables use probability masses; continuous variables use densities whose integrals over intervals give probabilities. A density itself can exceed one.

Conditioning changes the question

P(A|B) means probability of A given B. Bayes’ rule connects it to P(B|A), P(A), and P(B). Independence means observing one variable does not change the distribution of the other under the model. Correlation captures a narrower kind of association.

Mean, variance, and sampling

Expectation is a probability-weighted average. Variance describes dispersion around the mean. A sample mean estimates a population mean, with uncertainty depending on sample size and dependence. Duplicated records do not provide as much independent evidence as new observations.

Interpret intervals carefully

A frequentist confidence procedure has a specified long-run coverage under assumptions. A Bayesian credible interval summarizes a posterior under a likelihood and prior. Neither fixes dataset bias. Evaluation uncertainty includes sampling variation, annotation disagreement, and shifts between test data and deployment.

Worked example

Suppose a rare event occurs in 1% of cases. A detector catches 90% of events but flags 5% of non-events. Out of 10,000 cases it finds about 90 true positives and 495 false positives. Only 90/585≈15.4% of alerts are true positives.

What goes wrong

Confusing P(alert|event) with P(event|alert) ignores the base rate. A precise estimate on an unrepresentative dataset can be precisely wrong.

Check your understanding

Does a 95% accurate classifier prove useful when 99% of cases are negative?

Reveal the explanation

No. Always predicting negative already achieves 99% accuracy. Examine precision, recall, decision costs, and the actual class distribution.

How the pieces connect

Define event → Model uncertainty → Estimate → Decide. Each transition is a place where an assumption can be inspected before the next layer of the system compounds it.

An operating model for probability, statistics & uncertainty

Probability is useful because it forces a conditional statement. “The model is 90% accurate” is incomplete without the population, label definition, base rate, threshold, and time period. A probability estimate supports a decision only if it is calibrated enough for the decision costs and remains valid after deployment shifts.

The diagram is deliberately sequential, but real systems loop. A surprising result may expose a bad representation; a production incident may reveal a missing evaluation slice; a performance limit may require an algorithmic change. The point is to preserve the link between the abstract concept, the evidence you observe, and the decision you make next.

Worked system: an alert is a decision under a base rate

Suppose an account-abuse detector flags 100 accounts in a day. If 80 are truly abusive, its precision is 80%; if there were 160 abusive accounts in total, its recall is 50%. Those two facts immediately suggest different interventions: a costly manual review process may tolerate low recall but needs high precision; an automated block may demand an even lower false-positive rate; a low-friction warning can be used at a different threshold. Accuracy alone conceals all of this because legitimate accounts are usually the overwhelming majority.

Calibration matters when a score is presented as a probability. Among accounts given a 0.20 risk score, roughly one in five should be abusive if the score is calibrated for that population and time period. A model can rank cases well yet be poorly calibrated after a policy or user population changes. That is why probability is not just a number from a model—it is a claim about a conditional frequency, a population, and a decision that must survive deployment.

Notebook: Check the quantity before trusting it

Use this as an inspection pattern, not a drop-in production implementation. The specific values will change, but the habit remains: expose the assumption, calculate the boundary, and preserve the evidence that supports the next decision.

import numpy as np
x = np.array([2., -1.])
W = np.array([[1., 3.], [0., -2.]])
y = W @ x
print("shape", y.shape, "value", y)
# Write units and axis meanings beside every array.
What to test next. 1. Define event: State the population, outcome, and time horizon. 2. Model uncertainty: Choose conditional variables and assumptions. 3. Estimate: Use samples with known selection and dependence. 4. Decide: Combine uncertainty with costs and thresholds.

A rigorous way to practice

  1. Define event. State the population, outcome, and time horizon.
  2. Model uncertainty. Choose conditional variables and assumptions.
  3. Estimate. Use samples with known selection and dependence.
  4. Decide. Combine uncertainty with costs and thresholds.

For every rate, record both numerator and denominator. Then slice by the groups, time windows, and operating conditions that could change the denominator.

Questions that keep the chapter honest

AskWhy it mattersEvidence to collect
What assumptions does this method make?Every method encodes a view of data, hardware, or behavior.Inputs, representations, constraints, and cases outside the expected range.
What would make the result fail?Failure modes show where an aggregate result is fragile.Boundary cases, counterexamples, slices, and perturbations.
What decision changes if it improves?A metric only matters through an operational action.Baseline, threshold, cost, latency, and human-review consequences.
